analysis.one_liner: Counts staffed, leased, and temp workers' service toward employer pension and health benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote: referred to the Senate labor committee in July 2000, it never received a hearing or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies increasingly pay workers through staffing agencies, leasing firms, or payroll accounts, then label them 'temporary' or 'contractors' so they can be left out of pension and health plans that other employees doing the same work receive. This bill would amend the federal employee-benefits law so that all service to an employer counts toward benefit eligibility, ban plan provisions that exclude workers merely because of a label, void waivers workers were made to sign, and give courts a way to fix the mislabeling.
analysis.who_benefits: Contingent workers — people supplied by temp and staffing firms, leased employees, and workers labeled contractors who really work under an employer's direction — would count their service toward pension and welfare plan eligibility, join plans alongside coworkers doing the same work, and gain a legal route to recover benefits that mislabeling cost them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Temp, leased, and mislabeled contract workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires that service to an employer under common-law employment count toward plan eligibility regardless of whether the worker is paid through a staffing firm, payroll agency, or non-payroll account [S3].
Bars pension plans from excluding a common-law employee who performs the same or substantially the same work as enrolled employees, no matter what worker category the plan lists as ineligible [S3].
Makes any waiver of plan participation ineffective if it is tied to the miscategorization of the employee's status [S3].

Requires plan documents to use uniform, objective eligibility criteria rather than simply listing categories of excluded workers, and adds an enforcement route for workers who were miscategorized [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use contingent labor arrangements to keep workers out of benefit plans, and the staffing, temporary-help, and employee-leasing firms whose contracts help create that appearance, would bear the cost of enrolling these workers in pension and health coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Staffing firms and employers using contingent labor

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on employers and staffing firms, and some of that cost could be passed along by reducing contingent workers' pay rates or using fewer of them, rather than absorbed by the company [S3].

The bill relies on the common-law employment test to decide who counts as an employee, which would create litigation over borderline arrangements — genuinely independent contractors who do not perform the same work as employees are not covered, but the line would be contested in court [S3].

Critics of extending benefits rules to staffing arrangements argued it could raise the cost of flexible and temporary work arrangements, which some workers and businesses use by choice; this objection is not addressed in the provided record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a specific and growing group of workers: people who work full-time for one employer but are denied the pension and health coverage their coworkers receive because of how the paperwork is structured. The cost is real but conventional — it is the cost of extending to mislabeled workers the same benefits the employer already provides to comparable employees. The bill is a targeted anti-workaround measure rather than a broad mandate, which limits both its cost and its reach.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and nothing ever happened to it; when the Congress ended in January 2001 the bill was dead with no hearing, no vote, and no companion action.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on July 27, 2000, with Sens. Torricelli and Harkin as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill's entire recorded history is introduction and referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Staffing, temporary-help, and employee-leasing firms and the employers that use them to keep workers out of benefit plans were better off, since the practice the bill targeted faced no new federal restrictions. Contingent workers gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Staffing firms and employers using contingent labor

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its findings on contingent-worker mislabeling, and spoke on the record at introduction

for.name: Sens. Robert Torricelli (NJ) and Tom Harkin (IA)

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 27, 2000 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and the bill died in a Republican-run committee without any recorded vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: Their business model involves placing workers at client companies while keeping them off the client's benefit plans; the bill counts those workers' service toward the client employer's plans and invalidates waiver paperwork. Workers placed this way would gain coverage these firms' contracts currently let employers withhold.

industries.industry: Employers that rely on contingent labor
industries.note: Companies that label workers temporary or contract to exclude them from pension and welfare plans would have to enroll those who do the same work as regular employees, raising benefit costs. The bill's findings describe plan amendments and waiver documents designed to keep such workers out.
